4. The defendant. Nos. 2 and 3 (hereinafter opposite party Nos. 9-10 contested the suit by filing a, written statement, denying all the material allegations made in the plaint, contending inter alias, that the suit is not maintainable in the present form and the same is barred by limitation; that RS and SA record were prepared in the names of defendants on consideration of their right, title, interest and possession; that the processes of Rent Suit No. 4781 of 1934 and Rent Execution Case No. 1350 of 1935 were duly served upon the debtors; that Syed Abdus Sattar, predecessor of the contesting defendants owned the suit land by dint of purchase in auction on 15-11-1935; that the auction sale was confirmed on 7-1-1936 and delivery of possession was made on 26-5-1936; that the heirs of Edel Sharif filed a case under section 173(3) of the BT Act for setting aside the auction sale held in the aforesaid Rent Suit and the suit was dismissed on contest on 21-7-36; that the name of Abdul Jabbar was not mutated in the office of the superior landlord; that no notice under section 26C of the BT Act was given to the landlord informing of transfer made in favour of Abdul Jabbar that the heirs of Abdul Jabbar were not necessary parties in the rent suit; that the deceased Syed Abdus Sattar instituted Title Suit No. 251 of 1939 in the Sixth Court of Munsif, Barisal for the purpose of evicting the heirs of Edel Sharif from the suit land; that the suit was decreed; that the plaintiffs have got no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land; and that the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 Failure to give notice of succession as provided by section 15, if exonerates the Landlord, to make the successor a party to a rent suit, if the landlord otherwise gets notice of succession. 

 The failure to give notice of the succession as directed by section 15, Bengal Tenancy Act, does not exonerate the land lord from making the tenant a party to the suit for rent, if the landlord otherwise comes to know of the succession. The third clause of sub-section (3) of section 46A speaks of notice under section 15; but that does not mean that if the landlord other-wise gets the notice, he is not bound to make him a party. The general rule is that in a suit for rent all the landlords and all the tenants should be made parties. Section 146A comes as an exception to that general rule to meet cases where it may be difficult for the landlord to find out all the co-sharer tenants. " 

 In case of a transfer if the landlord has not been notified as required in clause (iii) of subsection (3) of section 146A the landlord is not bound to make him a party in a rent suit and if sale takes place in his absence, the tenancy shall in terms of sub-sections (2) and (3) be deemed to have been represented and the sale will be a rent sale. 

 Section 146A of the Bengal Tenancy Act the provision of which is applicable in this particular case, says that there must be relationship between the landlord and tenant and it further provides how the tenancy is represented, transferee who has gone to the extent that even has not notified in terms of section 26C or who has not noticed in terms of section 15 and whose name does not appear in the land-lord's rent roll need not be made a party in a rent suit and minus them the tenancy will still be represented." 

 17. The defendants claimed their right, title, interest and possession over the suit land on the basis of auction purchase made in the rent suit and subsequent transfer has been made to them by the auction purchaser Syed Abdus Sattar on 12-1-1973 by registered kabala, marked as Exhibit A. It appears that on behalf of the defendants a series of documents have been filed and marked as Exhibits A-G(4). 

 18. On critical analysis of the evidence on record, I find that both the Courts below concurrently held that the suit land was actually sold in auction and the auction purchaser Syed Abdus Sattar purchased it in open auction. It further appears that both the Courts below concurrently relied upon the Exhibit B Sale certificate of the land by which Syed Abdus Sattar purchased the suit land on 15-11-1935. Exhibit C, Miscellaneous Case No. 298 of 1996 under section 174(3) of the BT Act for setting aside the auction sale and the case was dismissed on contest. Exhibit C(1) writ of the delivery of possession on which that possession of the suit land was handed over to the auction purchaser on 29-6-1936. 

 19. It further appears that the plaintiffs claiming their right, title and interest only upon the Exhibit 1, save and except the said document they have no other supporting papers to show that after purchase the plaintiffs tried to pay rent and to get necessary right over the suit land. Furthermore, it has come to notice that the defendants' predecessors possessed the suit land by purchasing the same in auction and the defendants also got possession over the same. On perusal of the documentary and oral evidence on record, the defendants are found in possession as such the plaintiffs' suit for declaration without having prayer for recovery of khas possession in the suit land, the suit is not maintainable in the present form. Having regard to the facts I am in agreement with the concurrent finding of facts arrived at by the Courts below. 

 "A revision court acts beyond its jurisdiction in setting aside concurrent finding of fact, when there is no misreading and misappreciation of the evidence on record." 

 23. In the case of Abdul Matin Chowdhury vs Chapala Rani Sen and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 205, it is held that concurrent finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court and the First Appellate Court is binding upon the High Court Division in a second appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or of procedure which had affected the merit of the case. Similar views were taken in the cases of Abdul Mutaleb vs Md Mustakim Ali and others reported in 1999 BLD (AD) 156 and Abdul Mannan Khan and others vs Bangladesh and others reported in 38 DLR (AD) 201.
